title: Commutes Sentence of Darrell Frazier
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Darrell Frazier as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On Jan. 19, 2021, President Donald Trump commuted Darrell Frazier’s federal sentences, according to the Justice Department’s clemency list. It records two cases: a life sentence for a cocaine conspiracy in Tennessee and a consecutive 18-month sentence for a heroin conspiracy in Georgia. The Georgia case also carried six years of supervised release. The public list does not state the replacement terms.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Darrell Frazier
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Darrell Frazier as part of a clemency list.

notes: Read the linked DOJ commutations page. It identifies Frazier’s two federal cases, underlying offenses, original sentence terms, and the Jan. 19, 2021 clemency date, but does not give the commuted terms or a rationale. The source therefore supports a concise event account but not a full explanation of the practical effect.
proposed_correction: Add the terms in the signed commutation instrument and any published rationale; until then, keep the item limited to the documented grant and original sentences.

title: Commutes Sentence of Dwayne Phelps
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Dwayne Phelps as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department lists Dwayne Phelps among the people whose sentences Donald Trump commuted on Jan. 19, 2021. Phelps had received 240 months in prison and 10 years of supervised release for a methamphetamine distribution conspiracy in the Southern District of Indiana. The DOJ entry gives the original sentence and conviction, but does not identify the reduced term or explain the decision.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Dwayne Phelps
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Dwayne Phelps as part of a clemency list.

notes: Read the linked DOJ commutations page. It identifies the Southern District of Indiana case, the methamphetamine conspiracy, the original 240-month prison sentence and 10-year supervised-release term, and the clemency date. It does not state the replacement terms or a case-specific reason for the commutation, leaving the practical outcome unclear.

title: D.C. AG Sues Trump Inaugural Committee Over Hotel Payments
description_short: The D.C. attorney general sued the Trump inaugural committee and Trump’s hotel, alleging nonprofit funds were used to enrich the president’s business.
description_medium: In January 2020, D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine sued the Trump inaugural committee and Trump hotel, alleging the committee overpaid for inauguration event space with nonprofit funds. The complaint said the committee spent $1.03 million despite warnings that the hotel’s rates were above market. The committee said its independent audit found the spending lawful; Racine sought to recover the money for the nonprofit.
description_long: On Jan. 22, 2020, D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine sued the 58th Presidential Inaugural Committee and Trump International Hotel, alleging the committee improperly used nonprofit funds to benefit Donald Trump’s private business. The complaint said the committee spent $1.03 million for event space around Trump’s inauguration without seeking a fair market rate. According to the lawsuit, an event planner warned that the hotel’s initial $3.6 million quote for eight days and a later rate of $175,000 per day were far above comparable prices. A nonprofit hosting an inaugural prayer breakfast reportedly paid $5,000 for a ballroom the committee was charged $175,000 to use. Rick Gates negotiated the arrangements; the complaint said a planner raised the pricing with Gates, Trump and Ivanka Trump before the committee proceeded. The committee maintained that an independent audit found its finances lawful. Racine’s office sought to recover the funds under D.C. law barring nonprofit spending that benefits private parties. These were allegations in a civil suit; the linked reports do not give its final outcome.

preserved_fields.title: D.C. AG Sues Trump Inaugural Committee Over Hotel Payments
preserved_fields.description_short: The D.C. attorney general sued the Trump inaugural committee and Trump’s hotel, alleging nonprofit funds were used to enrich the president’s business.

notes: The linked reports describe the complaint and the committee’s response; no case disposition is asserted.

title: Elon Musk Reinstates Trump’s Twitter Account
description_short: Elon Musk announced Trump’s Twitter account would be reinstated after a poll on the platform.
description_medium: On Nov. 19, 2022, Elon Musk said Twitter would restore Donald Trump’s account after a 24-hour poll ended with a majority favoring reinstatement. The account was live soon afterward, though Trump did not immediately post. Twitter had permanently suspended him after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack, citing a risk of further incitement of violence.
description_long: Elon Musk announced the reversal on Nov. 19, 2022, less than a month after his $44 billion acquisition of Twitter closed. He had run a platform poll asking whether Donald Trump should return; it remained open for 24 hours, and Musk said the result favored reinstatement. He posted, “The people have spoken. Trump will be reinstated,” and the account appeared live shortly afterward. Trump did not post immediately. Twitter’s previous management had permanently suspended his account in January 2021 after the attack on the U.S. Capitol, saying his posts created a risk of further incitement of violence. The decision restored access to a major social platform for a former president who had since launched his own network. Before the poll, Trump had said he would not return to Twitter. The reinstatement was a platform-governance decision by Musk as the new owner; the linked report records the poll and change in access, but does not establish that Trump resumed using the account or describe the later effects of the restoration.

preserved_fields.title: Elon Musk Reinstates Trump’s Twitter Account
preserved_fields.description_short: Elon Musk announced Trump’s Twitter account would be reinstated after a poll on the platform.

notes: The invalid prior category “Social Media” was replaced with the permitted category Press Freedom. Description is limited to the timing, poll, prior suspension rationale, and immediate restoration reported by CNBC.

title: Trump Claims 32,000 Protesters Killed in Iran, Citing Disputed Figures
description_short: Trump said 32,000 people were killed in Iran's unrest and claimed his threats stopped mass hangings; monitors reported far lower verified totals.
description_medium: At a Feb. 20, 2026, briefing on the Supreme Court’s tariff ruling, Trump said 32,000 people had been killed in Iran’s recent protest crackdown without naming a source. CBS reported earlier estimates of 12,000–20,000 and noted that an internet blackout obscured the toll. Trump also said his threats stopped the execution of 837 people, a claim he qualified as “supposedly.”
description_long: Trump made the 32,000-death claim during a Feb. 20, 2026, briefing about the Supreme Court decision striking down his tariffs. CBS News reported that he did not identify a source and that the number was much higher than previously reported. Two sources, including one inside Iran, had told CBS that 12,000 to 20,000 people were killed during the January protests and government crackdown. An internet blackout made the full toll difficult to establish; Jan. 8 and 9 were described as especially deadly. In the same briefing, Trump said Iranian authorities had planned to hang 837 people and that he warned Iran it would be struck if executions went ahead. He said the executions were stopped, while qualifying that account with “supposedly.” The statement came as he urged Iran to negotiate over its nuclear program and said he was considering a limited military strike; U.S. forces were building up in the region. The linked report distinguishes Trump’s unsourced death toll and account of the threatened executions from the earlier casualty estimates. The figures and account of halted executions should therefore remain attributed claims, not established totals or independently confirmed outcomes.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Claims 32,000 Protesters Killed in Iran, Citing Disputed Figures
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump said 32,000 people were killed in Iran's unrest and claimed his threats stopped mass hangings; monitors reported far lower verified totals.

notes: Read the linked CBS News report; Reuters returned HTTP 401 in this pass. The account keeps the death toll and halted-execution statement attributed to Trump and the lower estimates attributed to CBS’s sources.
